title: Catchment selection changed the evidence for a demand-response rise in south-east Australian dry-spell fits
abstract: We test whether dry-spell flow decline became more sensitive to potential evaporation after 1997. We use CAMELS-AUS v2.03 and fit five-day decline against within-month demand anomalies, starting flow, season and prior rain in each era. In 189 mainland south-east Australian catchments, the 2010-2021 minus 1951-1996 demand slope was +0.01328 per mm/day, with approximate spatial and five-year score limits -0.00386 to +0.02670. The decline rise at the lower quartile of dry-event demand anomalies was +0.02625 (+0.00733 to +0.05287). SILO rain and Morton demand checks retained this distinction. A monthly-control fit kept 146 catchments and gave a positive slope interval. A post-result paired test on those same 146 catchments also gave a positive interval with the original seasonal controls. Their model difference was not clear. Thus catchment selection changes the evidence for a demand-response rise. The full-sample null cannot establish unchanged sensitivity across the region. Potential evaporation is not actual ET. The bounded decline index, common marginal support, short later era and approximate uncertainty limit physical claims. This test does not identify the cause of annual runoff loss. Code, source hashes, fit estimates, all combined uncertainty draws, audits and a figure are included.

display.caption: Era changes in the five-day decline demand slope and standardized decline. Bars use combined spatial resampling and common five-year score perturbations. Low demand means the lower quartile among dry-event anomalies, usually above the full-month mean. Cohorts differ. The late-spell test has only nine stations.

The primary 189-station slope interval includes zero. On the same 146 all-month stations, both seasonal models give positive intervals and similar estimates. This check was added after the main results.
